stem:
A 26-year-old man is admitted to your consultation-liaison psychiatry service under the mental health team after 3 days of mutism, refusal to eat and rigid posturing in his outpatient community rehabilitation home. He has known schizoaffective disorder well maintained on aripiprazole for 3 years without prior episodes of catatonia. His family denies illicit substance use in the last month and there has been no recent medication change.

On examination he is alert but immobile with waxy flexibility, echolalia when direct questions are repeated and periods of stereotyped facial grimacing. He resists positioning of his arms after a delay. His vital signs are stable. Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, creatine kinase, thyroid function and urine drug screen are within normal limits. Non-contrast computed tomography of the head is unremarkable. He has a documented allergy to haloperidol (dystonia) but no benzodiazepine history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility, echolalia when questions repeated, stereotyped grimacing, delayed resistance to passive positioning
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, CK, TFTs and urine drug screen within normal limits; non-contrast CT head unremarkable

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg and reassess the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale after 10 to 15 minutes
options.rationale: The AU standard is a 1 to 2 mg IV lorazepam challenge with reassessment at 10 to 15 minutes; a clear reduction on the Bush-Francis scale supports catatonia and predicts response to scheduled benzodiazepine. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous haloperidol 5 mg immediately for behavioural containment and psychosis in the same dose interval
options.rationale: Haloperidol worsens catatonia and can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; antipsychotic monotherapy is contraindicated until catatonia resolves. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy this afternoon without further trial of pharmacological treatment first
options.rationale: ECT is second-line after benzodiazepine trial has failed or when malignant catatonia is present; the initial step is a lorazepam challenge. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Start intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg per kilogram to treat suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome as first therapy
options.rationale: CK, temperature and autonomic vitals are normal; NMS is unlikely and dantrolene does not address benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Initiate intravenous olanzapine 10 mg with intramuscular midazolam sedation to manage acute behavioural presentation
options.rationale: Adding a second antipsychotic worsens catatonia and IM midazolam obscures the diagnostic challenge; scheduled lorazepam is the correct first-line trial. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor disturbance defined by three or more of stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerisms, stereotypies, agitation, grimacing, echolalia or echopraxia (DSM-5-TR). It occurs in mood, psychotic and medical conditions. Initial assessment must exclude a delirium precipitant and NMS with FBC, UEC, CK, TFT, drug screen and imaging. A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM) with reassessment at 10 to 15 minutes on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is both diagnostic and therapeutic; positive responders receive scheduled lorazepam 1 to 4 mg every 4 to 8 hours titrated to response. Electroconvulsive therapy is second-line after benzodiazepine trial failure or first-line in malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rigidity).
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale objectifies severity and response.
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic.
Antipsychotic monotherapy is contraindicated during active catatonia.
ECT for benzodiazepine failure or malignant catatonia.
explanation.pearls: For a first episode of catatonia, give IV lorazepam 1 to 2 mg and reassess the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale at 10 to 15 minutes; escalate to scheduled dosing if there is objective improvement.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by ambulance 90 minutes after an intentional ingestion of approximately 60 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets, taken with vodka. Her partner found her drowsy at home. She has a history of borderline personality disorder and prior self-harm by cutting. Her only medication is amitriptyline 50 mg at night for chronic tension headache.

On assessment she is drowsy and responsive only to voice, with dry mucous membranes and warm dry skin. Pupils are 6 mm and sluggishly reactive. There is no focal neurology. Bedside ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 130/min with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 30 mmHg, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L (22-30) and lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Point-of-care glucose is 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-6.0). She weighs 65 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but responds to voice, dry mucous membranes, warm dry skin, dilated sluggish pupils, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 140 ms with 4 mm terminal R in aVR, sinus tachycardia; venous gas pH 7.28, HCO3 16 mmol/L (22-30), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-6.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to 1 mg total to reverse the sedation and improve airway protection
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose with pro-convulsant tricyclics; it may precipitate seizures and unmask cardiovascular toxicity. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose

options.text: Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 2 mmol per kilogram bolus, aiming for QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms and terminal R in aVR above 3 mm meet AU criteria for hypertonic bicarbonate; 1 to 2 mmol/kg boluses with target pH 7.50 to 7.55 improve conduction. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 5 mg titrated to sedation for the anticholinergic delirium and expected withdrawal
options.rationale: Diazepam does not address the sodium channel blockade driving the wide complex tachycardia and hypotension; hypertonic bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine 1 mg over 5 minutes to reverse the anticholinergic component of the overdose picture
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in tricyclic overdose because it can precipitate seizures and asystole; bicarbonate is the antidote for cardiotoxicity. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose

options.text: Intravenous 20 percent intralipid emulsion 1.5 mL per kilogram bolus as first-line antidote before bicarbonate
options.rationale: Intralipid is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to bicarbonate; first-line antidote is hypertonic bicarbonate for the wide QRS. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose produces anticholinergic, sodium channel blocking, potassium channel blocking and alpha-adrenergic effects, with cardiovascular toxicity as the main driver of death (wide QRS, terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia). QRS above 100 ms predicts seizure and above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia. The AU antidote is hypertonic sodium bicarbonate (8.4 percent) 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to target arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55 or QRS narrowing below 100 ms, followed by infusion; intubation and hyperventilation to a pCO2 of 30 mmHg supports alkalinisation. Seizures are treated with benzodiazepines and intralipid is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Physostigmine and flumazenil are contraindicated because they precipitate seizure and dysrhythmia.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms and terminal R in aVR above 3 mm mark cardiotoxicity.
Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg is first-line antidote.
Target arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55 or QRS below 100 ms.
Avoid physostigmine and flumazenil in TCA overdose.
explanation.pearls: For TCA overdose with QRS above 100 ms and terminal R in aVR above 3 mm, give hypertonic sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and target pH 7.50 to 7.55 with QRS narrowing.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose
NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA Overdose

stem:
A 28-year-old software engineer presents to your general practice requesting an ADHD assessment. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, chronic procrastination and losing personal items, dating back to primary school reports of daydreaming in class. She has managed academically but describes constant last-minute crisis work and increasing job stress. She has one previous episode of major depression 5 years ago that responded to sertraline for 12 months and no other psychiatric history. She drinks 10 standard drinks per week and does not use illicit substances.

On examination she is well groomed and organised for the appointment. Mental state is euthymic with no psychosis and no active suicidality. Her physical examination and vital signs are unremarkable. She has brought school reports and a parent-completed retrospective report scored as suggestive of childhood inattentive presentation. She has no personal history of cardiovascular disease and no family history of sudden cardiac death.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well groomed, euthymic mental state, no thought disorder, insight preserved, no cardiovascular findings

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily to observe symptomatic response and confirm the diagnosis on treatment
options.rationale: Only Australian consultant psychiatrists or paediatricians can initiate stimulants for adult ADHD under state authority arrangements; symptomatic trial by GP is not authorised. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Order neuropsychological testing today and interpret the results in general practice before further specialist referral
options.rationale: Neuropsychology is adjunctive; the AU pathway is a psychiatrist- or paediatrician-led diagnostic interview with collateral, not a neuropsychology-first workup. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Refer to a consultant psychiatrist with a specific interest in adult ADHD for structured diagnostic interview and stimulant authority
options.rationale: Under the AU Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD, only consultant psychiatrists or paediatricians can diagnose and initiate stimulant therapy; GP refers with collateral. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Reintroduce sertraline 50 mg daily and reassess in 6 to 8 weeks assuming the current picture is depressive relapse
options.rationale: She is euthymic with no depressive symptoms; sertraline does not treat ADHD and would not address the presenting complaint. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Provide reassurance that her presentation is common workplace stress and recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone as sufficient care
options.rationale: CBT is a component of ADHD care but denying assessment when childhood documented history supports ADHD misses a treatable condition. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires childhood onset (before 12 years) of five or more inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms causing functional impairment in at least two settings. The Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD reserves diagnosis and stimulant initiation to consultant psychiatrists or paediatricians authorised under state schedules. General practitioners provide the referral with collateral (childhood school reports, parent-completed retrospective questionnaires) and manage stable ongoing prescriptions once a shared-care plan is in place. Baseline assessment before stimulants includes cardiovascular history and examination, blood pressure and pulse, and ECG only where cardiac risk factors are present. First-line pharmacotherapy is a psychostimulant (methylphenidate or dexamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine); atomoxetine or guanfacine are non-stimulant alternatives.
key_points: AU requires psychiatrist or paediatrician for diagnosis and stimulant initiation.
GP role: referral with collateral, then shared care.
Baseline cardiovascular history, examination, BP, pulse before stimulants.
Non-stimulant options: atomoxetine, guanfacine.
explanation.pearls: When an Australian adult presents with a plausible ADHD history, refer to a consultant psychiatrist or paediatrician with collateral evidence; only they can initiate stimulant therapy under state authority.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

stem:
A 19-year-old university student is brought to your urgent care clinic by his housemates after 5 days of paranoid beliefs that Australian Security Intelligence Organisation agents are surveilling him through his laptop camera. He has been using high-potency edible cannabis products daily for 4 months, most recently increasing to twice daily. He has no personal or family psychiatric history. His father has type 2 diabetes but there are no other medical conditions.

On examination he is anxious but engageable, oriented to time, place and person. Speech is coherent but pressured. He describes persecutory delusions and reports hearing his neighbours talk about him through the walls when they are demonstrably away at work. Insight is limited. Physical examination is unremarkable with a mildly elevated heart rate. Urine drug screen is positive for tetrahydrocannabinol only. Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function and non-contrast computed tomography head are within normal limits. He has never seen a psychiatrist before.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Anxious, oriented, pressured coherent speech, persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, limited insight
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for THC only; FBC, UEC, TFTs and CT head within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological and disposition plan?

options.text: Discharge home with 3 days of oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily to manage cannabis withdrawal only and no antipsychotic
options.rationale: Active psychotic symptoms warrant antipsychotic cover; benzodiazepines alone would not treat the delusions and hallucinations. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorder Guidance)

options.text: Commence oral clozapine 12.5 mg titrated up over 2 weeks as first-line antipsychotic for treatment-resistant psychosis
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after 2 adequate antipsychotic trials; using it first in a new presentation is not indicated. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorder Guidance)

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act and commence intramuscular depot risperidone microspheres 25 mg fortnightly from day 1
options.rationale: Depot antipsychotic initiation without an oral tolerance trial and without exhausting voluntary care options is not consistent with AU practice. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorder Guidance)

options.text: Refer for admission to a voluntary early psychosis inpatient bed, commence oral olanzapine 5 to 10 mg nightly and support cessation of cannabis
options.rationale: AU guidance recommends voluntary admission where possible, oral low-dose olanzapine (or aripiprazole) with cannabis cessation; symptoms often resolve over weeks and prognosis depends on abstinence. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorder Guidance)

options.text: Commence lithium carbonate 500 mg twice daily as mood stabiliser assuming underlying bipolar disorder with psychotic features
options.rationale: There are no manic or depressive features; lithium is not indicated for cannabis-induced psychosis without evidence of mood disorder. (Source: RANZCP Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorder Guidance)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder is defined by prominent psychotic symptoms developing during or within 1 month of cannabis use that are not better explained by a primary psychotic disorder. High-potency products, daily use and adolescent onset increase risk. Initial management is a low-dose oral second-generation antipsychotic (olanzapine or aripiprazole are common), voluntary admission where possible for containment and monitoring, and immediate cannabis cessation. Symptoms typically resolve over days to weeks, though up to 40 percent progress to a persistent psychotic disorder over time, so long-term follow-up in an early psychosis service is standard AU practice. Involuntary detention under the Mental Health Act is reserved for those who lack capacity and cannot be managed safely voluntarily.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychosis requires antipsychotic cover, not benzodiazepine alone.
Voluntary admission and low-dose olanzapine or aripiprazole are first-line.
Immediate cannabis cessation is central to recovery.
Up to 40 percent progress to persistent psychosis, warranting follow-up.
explanation.pearls: For high-potency cannabis-induced psychosis in a young person, admit voluntarily to an early psychosis service, start oral olanzapine 5 to 10 mg nightly and stop cannabis; symptoms usually clear within weeks.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is reviewed in your outpatient psychiatry clinic. She has been stable for 3 years on sodium valproate 1200 mg daily after two prior manic episodes with psychotic features. She is in a new relationship with her partner of 6 months and has stopped her copper intrauterine device 2 weeks ago because they are planning pregnancy in the next year. She has no other medical conditions and does not use any other prescribed or over-the-counter medications.

On examination she is euthymic with no evidence of mood elevation or depression, no psychotic symptoms and preserved insight. She reports adherence with valproate and finds it effective. She has never been prescribed lithium or lamotrigine. Her last serum valproate level was 84 mg/L (50-100). Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver enzymes and thyroid function are within normal limits. She is now asking whether she can continue valproate through pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic symptoms, insight preserved, no tremor, no gait disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate 84 mg/L (50-100); FBC, UEC, LFTs and TFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her mood stabiliser?

options.text: Continue valproate 1200 mg daily and add folic acid 5 mg daily preconception to reduce foetal neural tube defect risk
options.rationale: Folic acid at any dose does not neutralise the specific valproate risks of neural tube defects, dose-dependent cognitive impairment and autism spectrum disorder in exposed offspring; substitution is required. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily as a below-threshold dose that avoids teratogenicity while planning pregnancy
options.rationale: There is no safe dose of valproate in pregnancy; even low-dose exposure carries neurodevelopmental risk and does not adequately treat bipolar I. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue valproate throughout pregnancy but arrange first-trimester detailed anomaly ultrasound as risk mitigation only
options.rationale: Detection of abnormality after conception does not prevent teratogenicity; TGA and RANZCP require substitution before pregnancy where feasible in bipolar disorder. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Stop valproate and add quetiapine 300 mg nightly as monotherapy indefinitely and defer any pregnancy planning for 3 years
options.rationale: Quetiapine monotherapy is not first-line for bipolar I maintenance; lithium remains preferred for a woman with prior manic episodes planning pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Wean valproate and cross-titrate to lithium 750 mg nightly, aiming for a serum lithium 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L before conception
options.rationale: For an actively planning woman with bipolar I, lithium is a preferred alternative preconception because valproate has the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of the mood stabilisers under the AU Pregnancy Prevention Program requirements. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the mood stabilisers: neural tube defects (approximately 1 to 2 percent), craniofacial and limb anomalies, dose-dependent reduction in IQ (approximately 8 to 10 points), and increased autism spectrum disorder risk (about 4-fold). The TGA operates a Pregnancy Prevention Program requiring documented contraception for reproductive-age women on valproate; prescribers must switch to an alternative when pregnancy is planned. Lithium is a preferred alternative in bipolar I maintenance, with target level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L preconception. Ebstein anomaly risk with lithium (0.05 to 0.1 percent) is far lower than valproate's neurodevelopmental risks, and antenatal foetal echocardiography at 16 to 20 weeks screens for it. Lamotrigine is a further alternative particularly for bipolar depression predominance.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity: NTDs, cognitive impairment, autism (dose-dependent).
AU Pregnancy Prevention Program required for reproductive-age women.
Lithium (target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L) is preferred substitute in bipolar I.
Foetal echocardiography at 16 to 20 weeks screens for lithium-related Ebstein anomaly.
explanation.pearls: For a woman with bipolar I planning pregnancy on valproate, cross-titrate to lithium (target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L) before conception; there is no safe valproate dose in pregnancy.

sources.label: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
TGA Sodium Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program

stem:
A 42-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg nightly for 18 months with excellent symptom response and metabolic side effects only. His routine haematological monitoring today shows an absolute neutrophil count of 1.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), white cell count of 3.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets of 190 x10^9/L (150-400) and haemoglobin of 138 g/L (130-170). He is asymptomatic, afebrile and his mother says he has been better than she has ever seen him. He has never received granulocyte colony-stimulating factor.

On examination he is well, alert, oriented and stable. Vital signs are normal. There are no signs of infection, no oral ulceration and no rash. Prior monitoring bloods have shown ANC consistently 2.5 to 4.0 x10^9/L. He lives independently in supported accommodation with weekly community mental health nurse visits. He is not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background and no benign ethnic neutropenia has been documented.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well, alert, oriented, no infection focus, no oral ulceration, no rash

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the full blood count with differential within 24 hours to trend the neutrophil count
options.rationale: An ANC in the Amber range (1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L) does not require immediate cessation on Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring System criteria; twice-weekly monitoring continues and cessation only occurs if ANC falls below 1.0. (Source: Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring System)

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and admit for daily full blood count monitoring until ANC recovers above 3.0 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Amber-range ANC (1.0 to 1.5) does not require cessation on the AU CPMS; stopping prematurely risks psychotic relapse in a well-controlled patient. (Source: Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring System)

options.text: Continue clozapine at reduced dose 200 mg nightly for the next fortnight and repeat full blood count monthly instead of weekly
options.rationale: Dose reduction and less frequent monitoring do not reflect Amber protocol; ANC does not track linearly with dose and less monitoring is unsafe. (Source: Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring System)

options.text: Commence subcutaneous filgrastim 300 micrograms daily as prophylactic G-CSF before any dose or monitoring change
options.rationale: G-CSF is reserved for severe neutropenia (ANC below 0.5) or clozapine-induced agranulocytosis, not Amber-range readings. (Source: Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring System)

options.text: Cease clozapine permanently and cross-titrate to intramuscular paliperidone palmitate 100 mg monthly given the risk of agranulocytosis
options.rationale: Permanent discontinuation is only mandated after ANC below 1.0 (Red) or agranulocytosis; premature switching loses the treatment-resistant response he has achieved. (Source: Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring System)

explanation.summary: Clozapine haematological monitoring in Australia is governed by the Clozapine Patient Monitoring System (CPMS) with a traffic-light protocol on absolute neutrophil count. Green (ANC at or above 2.0) permits routine weekly monitoring for the first 18 weeks then monthly. Amber (ANC 1.0 to 1.5, or WCC 3.0 to 3.5) allows continuation with twice-weekly monitoring until values return to Green. Red (ANC below 1.0, or WCC below 3.0) mandates immediate cessation, daily monitoring and mandatory reporting; rechallenge is generally not permitted after clozapine-induced agranulocytosis (ANC below 0.5). Benign ethnic neutropenia (common in some African, Middle Eastern and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations) may allow modified thresholds after haematology consultation. G-CSF is reserved for Red readings or severe agranulocytosis.
key_points: CPMS traffic light: Green >=2.0, Amber 1.0-1.5, Red <1.0.
Amber allows continuation with twice-weekly monitoring.
Red mandates cessation, daily monitoring and reporting.
Benign ethnic neutropenia may allow modified thresholds.
explanation.pearls: For clozapine-treated patients with ANC 1.2 x10^9/L (Amber), continue clozapine and repeat FBC within 24 hours; cessation only occurs when ANC falls below 1.0 (Red).

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
A 45-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder is brought to your emergency department by his wife after 6 hours of confusion, agitation and shaking. He had olanzapine 15 mg nightly for 5 years without change. Three days ago his general practitioner prescribed venlafaxine 75 mg daily for a superimposed depressive episode; he took his first dose 3 days ago, has escalated with an extra tablet on his own initiative today. This afternoon he also took 2 tablets of tramadol 50 mg for back pain, and one of his wife's linezolid tablets for a chest infection because he assumed it would help.

On examination he is diaphoretic, agitated and disoriented to time. His tone is markedly increased in the lower limbs with clonus at both ankles far exceeding the upper limbs, and hyperactive tendon reflexes throughout. Pupils are dilated at 6 mm and reactive. There is mild rigidity but no lead-pipe rigidity of the upper limbs. Creatine kinase is 780 U/L (30-200), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), venous pH 7.30, and urine drug screen is negative for stimulants.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 168/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, disoriented, lower limb clonus greater than upper limb, hyperreflexia, dilated reactive pupils, mild rigidity without lead-pipe
data_table.Investigations: CK 780 U/L (30-200); sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145); venous pH 7.30; urine drug screen negative for stimulants

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg per kilogram as first-line antidote for neuroleptic malignant syndrome from long-term olanzapine
options.rationale: NMS features are bradyreflexia and lead-pipe rigidity; here the lower-greater-than-upper clonus and hyperreflexia pattern with three new serotonergic drugs favours serotonin syndrome and dantrolene does not treat it. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Serotonin Syndrome)

options.text: Cease all serotonergic drugs, give intravenous benzodiazepine sedation and consider oral cyproheptadine 12 mg loading dose then 2 mg every 2 hours
options.rationale: Three new serotonergic agents (venlafaxine, tramadol, linezolid) plus the clonus-greater-in-lower-limbs pattern is serotonin syndrome; supportive care with benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine 12 mg load then 2 mg 2-hourly is the AU pathway. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Serotonin Syndrome)

options.text: Intramuscular bromocriptine 2.5 mg as a dopamine agonist to reverse suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome caused by olanzapine
options.rationale: Bromocriptine treats NMS; the clonus-predominant lower limb picture on new serotonergic agents supports serotonin syndrome, and dopamine agonists have no role there. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Serotonin Syndrome)

options.text: Restart oral olanzapine at reduced dose 5 mg immediately to control agitation and consider ECT if response is inadequate
options.rationale: Adding an antipsychotic worsens serotonin syndrome via alpha-1 blockade contributing to hyperthermia; ECT is not first-line here. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Serotonin Syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 2 mmol per kilogram bolus targeting an arterial pH of 7.50 for suspected cardiotoxicity
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is the antidote for sodium channel blocker toxicity (e.g. TCA overdose); it has no role in serotonin syndrome. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Serotonin Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and NMS overlap but differ in key features. Serotonin syndrome typically develops within hours of a new or additional serotonergic agent and features hyperreflexia, clonus that is more marked in the lower limbs than upper (a Hunter Criteria feature), diaphoresis, agitation, dilated reactive pupils, tachycardia and hyperthermia. NMS typically develops over days to weeks after initiation or dose increase of an antipsychotic and features lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, autonomic instability, altered mental status and markedly elevated CK. Treatment differs: serotonin syndrome is managed by ceasing the culprit drugs, benzodiazepine sedation and oral cyproheptadine 12 mg load then 2 mg every 2 hours (maximum 32 mg/day); NMS is managed by ceasing the antipsychotic, cooling, benzodiazepine, and dantrolene or bromocriptine if severe. Serotonergic combinations to avoid include SSRI/SNRI plus tramadol, linezolid, MAOI and dextromethorphan.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus lower-greater-than-upper, hyperreflexia, dilated reactive pupils.
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, days-to-weeks course, marked CK rise.
SS treatment: benzodiazepine sedation plus cyproheptadine 12 mg load then 2 mg 2-hourly.
NMS treatment: dantrolene or bromocriptine if severe.
explanation.pearls: For serotonin syndrome, stop all serotonergic agents, sedate with benzodiazepine and give oral cyproheptadine 12 mg load then 2 mg every 2 hours; dantrolene and bromocriptine belong to NMS.
